question.text: What is STE-80, and how do its rules make a technical instruction easier to read?
question.known_at: Caption 1 names the topic. The reason it matters comes at captions 6-7 ("so every word must help").
question.result_stated: Partly, at caption 25: "The bar counts words, but the goal is less work", with caption 23 "Sixteen words became nine."

reply.motive: Reason to care: "Manuals are read under time pressure, often in a second language, so every word must help" (captions 6-7). Reason for the approach (rewriting one sentence rule by rule): missing. The video never says why one worked example is used.
reply.close: Not really. The ending lists rules that were not shown ("short sentences, one meaning per word, and no filler") and does not come back to the motive or to what dropping the dictionary means. The closest general statement is caption 25: "the goal is less work".
reply.recap: STE-80 is a lighter version of Simplified Technical English: it uses plain words, gives direct commands and uses action verbs, so a hurried, non-native reader of a manual has less work to do.
reply.strongest: Captions 10-12 (rule one): the red-to-green swap of "replenished prior to commencing" into "full before starting". It is clear, it is shown and said at the same time, and the bar shows the small change.
reply.weakest: Captions 19-21 (rule three): the narration quotes phrases without quotation marks, the rewrite changes the meaning, and a noun change is filed under the verb rule.
suggestions: Explain what the ASD-STE100 approved dictionary is (a controlled list of allowed words, each with one meaning), so that dropping it means something.
Replace or remove "eighty percent of the way", or say how it is measured.
Name the rule-two change as 'use the imperative' instead of only 'cut the opening'.
Check that rule three keeps the meaning (for example 'Fill the reservoir if needed'), or say openly that the rewrite also makes the instruction clearer.
Move 'operation becomes the machine' under a rule about specific nouns, or under rule one.
End by restating the reader's problem (time pressure, second language) and how the three rules solve it, instead of listing new rules with no examples.
